item.title: Build an AI Agent Harness from Scratch: A Complete Course Tutorial
item.description: Learn to build an AI agent harness from scratch in Python — tool registry, LLM interface, conversation memory, and execution loop with full code examples.
item.content:encoded:
What is an Agent Harness?

An agent harness is the middleware layer that sits between a large language model (LLM) and your application logic. It handles tool discovery, model communication, conversation history, and the execution loop that makes autonomous agents possible. Instead of calling an LLM directly with a single prompt, a harness manages the full ask-generate-execute cycle — the LLM decides which tools to call, the harness executes them, and the results feed back into the next model turn. This separation of concerns is what turns a stateless API call into a reasoning agent that can browse the web, run code, query databases, and take actions on your behalf.

The concept has exploded in popularity. As of mid-2026, the OpenAI Agents SDK has surpassed 28,000 GitHub stars, and the broader ecosystem of agent harness projects — from Codex and Qwen Code to OpenHands and Hermes Agent — sees more than two new releases per day across major open-source projects. A 2026 survey paper titled “Code as Agent Harness” frames code itself as the operational substrate for agent reasoning, acting, environment modeling, and execution-based verification. Understanding how a harness works from the inside out is no longer optional for AI engineers — it is foundational.

The 4 Essential Components of Every Agent Harness

Every agent harness, regardless of complexity or provider, shares four core components. Whether you are building a simple CLI agent in 150 lines or a production-grade multi-agent orchestrator, these four pieces must exist in some form.

Tool Registry — Discovering and Describing Available Capabilities

The tool registry is the agent’s catalog of what it can do. Each tool is a function wrapped with a schema that the LLM can understand — typically a JSON schema describing the tool’s name, description, and parameters. When the LLM decides it needs to perform an action, it selects a tool from this registry and provides the arguments.

A well-designed tool registry supports:

  • Dynamic discovery: Tools can be registered at startup or discovered at runtime via a service registry (as demonstrated by the go-micro approach in the “Build Your Own AI Agent CLI” series).
  • Rich descriptions: Each tool includes a human-readable description that helps the LLM decide when to use it. The quality of these descriptions directly impacts the agent’s ability to choose the right tool.
  • Type-safe parameters: JSON Schema or Pydantic models define exactly what arguments each tool expects, enabling validation before execution.
  • Error contracts: Tools declare what errors they might return, allowing the harness to handle failures gracefully.

LLM Interface — Connecting to Any Provider

The LLM interface abstracts away the differences between model providers. A good harness supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, and local models through a unified API. This provider-agnostic design is critical because:

  • Different models excel at different tasks (Claude for coding, GPT-4o for reasoning, Gemini for multimodal).
  • Cost optimization requires routing simple tasks to cheaper models.
  • Resilience demands fallback chains when a provider is down.
  • Local models are essential for air-gapped or privacy-sensitive environments.

The interface typically handles: authentication, request formatting, response parsing, streaming, token counting, and error retry logic. The OpenAI Agents SDK, for example, supports 100+ LLMs through its LiteLLM integration while maintaining a single agent interface.

Conversation Memory — Managing Context Windows and History

Conversation memory is what gives an agent continuity across multiple turns. Without it, every LLM call is a fresh start — the agent cannot remember what it did two steps ago, what the user asked five minutes ago, or what results it already computed.

Memory management involves several challenges:

  • Context window limits: Even the largest models (Claude 4 with 200K tokens, Gemini 2.5 Pro with 2M tokens) have finite context. The harness must decide what to keep, what to summarize, and what to drop.
  • Token budgeting: Each turn consumes tokens from the context window. The harness needs to track usage and implement strategies like sliding windows, summarization, or retrieval-augmented memory.
  • Structured history: Raw message dumps waste tokens. A good harness stores structured turns — user message, assistant response, tool calls, tool results — and formats them efficiently for the model.

Execution Loop — The Core Ask-Generate-Execute Cycle

The execution loop is the heartbeat of the agent harness. It follows a simple but powerful pattern:

  1. Ask: Present the current state (system prompt + conversation history + tool schemas) to the LLM.
  2. Generate: The LLM responds — either with a final answer or with one or more tool call requests.
  3. Execute: The harness runs the requested tools, captures results, and appends them to the conversation history.
  4. Repeat: Go back to step 1 with the updated state.

This loop continues until the LLM produces a final answer, reaches a maximum iteration limit, or hits a safety guardrail. The elegance of this design is its simplicity — the entire complexity of autonomous agent behavior emerges from this single loop.

Building Your First Agent Harness — Step-by-Step Implementation in Python

Let’s build a working agent harness from scratch. We will implement all four components in under 200 lines of Python, then extend it with advanced features.

Setting Up the Project Structure

Create a new directory and a single Python file:

agent-harness/
├── harness.py          # Main harness implementation
├── tools/              # Tool definitions
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── web_search.py
│   └── calculator.py
├── requirements.txt    # Dependencies
└── example.py          # Usage example

Dependencies are minimal: openai (or anthropic), pydantic for schema validation, and httpx for async HTTP calls.

Implementing the Tool Registry

from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Callable, Dict, Any, List, Optional
import json


class ToolParameter(BaseModel):
    name: str
    type: str
    description: str
    required: bool = True


class Tool(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str
    parameters: List[ToolParameter]
    function: Callable

    def to_openai_tool(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """Convert to OpenAI-compatible tool schema."""
        properties = {}
        required_params = []
        for p in self.parameters:
            properties[p.name] = {
                "type": p.type,
                "description": p.description,
            }
            if p.required:
                required_params.append(p.name)
        return {
            "type": "function",
            "function": {
                "name": self.name,
                "description": self.description,
                "parameters": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": properties,
                    "required": required_params,
                },
            },
        }


class ToolRegistry:
    def __init__(self):
        self._tools: Dict[str, Tool] = {}

    def register(self, tool: Tool):
        self._tools[tool.name] = tool

    def get(self, name: str) -> Optional[Tool]:
        return self._tools.get(name)

    def list_schemas(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        return [t.to_openai_tool() for t in self._tools.values()]

    def execute(self, name: str, arguments: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
        tool = self.get(name)
        if not tool:
            return f"Error: Tool '{name}' not found"
        try:
            result = tool.function(**arguments)
            return str(result)
        except Exception as e:
            return f"Error executing {name}: {str(e)}"

This registry is the backbone of the harness. Tools are registered with their name, description, parameter schema, and the actual Python function. The to_openai_tool() method converts each tool into the format that OpenAI and compatible APIs expect, making integration seamless.

Creating the LLM Client Abstraction

from openai import OpenAI
from typing import List, Dict, Any, Optional


class LLMClient:
    def __init__(
        self,
        model: str = "gpt-4o",
        api_key: Optional[str] = None,
        base_url: Optional[str] = None,
    ):
        self.model = model
        self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key, base_url=base_url)

    def chat(
        self,
        messages: List[Dict[str, str]],
        tools: Optional[List[Dict[str, Any]]] = None,
        temperature: float = 0.7,
        max_tokens: int = 4096,
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        kwargs = {
            "model": self.model,
            "messages": messages,
            "temperature": temperature,
            "max_tokens": max_tokens,
        }
        if tools:
            kwargs["tools"] = tools
            kwargs["tool_choice"] = "auto"

        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)
        return response.choices[0].message

This abstraction lets you swap providers by changing the base_url and model parameters. For Anthropic, you would create a similar wrapper using the Anthropic SDK. For local models running through Ollama or vLLM, point base_url to http://localhost:11434/v1.

Building the Conversation Manager

from typing import List, Dict, Any


class ConversationManager:
    def __init__(self, system_prompt: str, max_history: int = 20):
        self.messages: List[Dict[str, Any]] = [
            {"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}
        ]
        self.max_history = max_history

    def add_user_message(self, content: str):
        self.messages.append({"role": "user", "content": content})
        self._trim()

    def add_assistant_message(self, content: Optional[str], tool_calls: Optional[List] = None):
        msg = {"role": "assistant"}
        if content:
            msg["content"] = content
        if tool_calls:
            msg["tool_calls"] = tool_calls
        self.messages.append(msg)
        self._trim()

    def add_tool_result(self, tool_call_id: str, name: str, result: str):
        self.messages.append({
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": tool_call_id,
            "name": name,
            "content": result,
        })
        self._trim()

    def get_messages(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
        return self.messages

    def _trim(self):
        """Keep system message + last N turns."""
        if len(self.messages) > self.max_history + 1:
            system = self.messages[0]
            self.messages = [system] + self.messages[-(self.max_history):]

The conversation manager maintains the message history, handles the system prompt, and implements a sliding window to stay within context limits. The _trim method drops the oldest messages while preserving the system prompt, ensuring the agent never exceeds its budget.

Wiring the Main Execution Loop

class AgentHarness:
    def __init__(
        self,
        llm: LLMClient,
        registry: ToolRegistry,
        conversation: ConversationManager,
        max_iterations: int = 10,
    ):
        self.llm = llm
        self.registry = registry
        self.conversation = conversation
        self.max_iterations = max_iterations

    def run(self, user_input: str) -> str:
        self.conversation.add_user_message(user_input)
        iteration = 0

        while iteration < self.max_iterations:
            iteration += 1
            messages = self.conversation.get_messages()
            tools = self.registry.list_schemas()

            response = self.llm.chat(messages, tools=tools)

            if not response.tool_calls:
                # LLM produced a final answer
                self.conversation.add_assistant_message(
                    content=response.content
                )
                return response.content

            # Process each tool call
            self.conversation.add_assistant_message(
                content=response.content,
                tool_calls=[
                    {
                        "id": tc.id,
                        "type": "function",
                        "function": {
                            "name": tc.function.name,
                            "arguments": tc.function.arguments,
                        },
                    }
                    for tc in response.tool_calls
                ],
            )

            for tc in response.tool_calls:
                import json
                args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments)
                result = self.registry.execute(tc.function.name, args)
                self.conversation.add_tool_result(tc.id, tc.function.name, result)

        return "Agent reached maximum iterations without producing a final answer."

This is the core loop. The harness sends the conversation state plus tool schemas to the LLM. If the LLM returns tool calls, the harness executes them and feeds the results back. If the LLM returns a text response, the harness returns it to the user. The max_iterations guard prevents infinite loops.

Adding Advanced Features

Once the basic loop works, you can extend the harness with production-grade capabilities.

Multi-Turn Conversations and Context Management

Real-world agents need to maintain state across multiple user interactions. Implement session persistence by serializing the conversation history to a database or file. Use summarization techniques — when the context window fills, ask a secondary LLM to summarize older turns, then replace them with the summary. This is how production systems like Hermes Agent handle long-running sessions without losing critical context.

Tool Execution with Error Handling

Tools can fail for many reasons: network timeouts, invalid inputs, rate limits, or unexpected data. A robust harness wraps each tool execution in try-catch blocks, returns structured error messages to the LLM, and implements retry logic with exponential backoff. The LLM can then decide whether to retry, try a different tool, or inform the user of the failure.

Streaming Responses

For a better user experience, stream the LLM’s response token by token. Instead of waiting for the full response, yield each chunk as it arrives. When the LLM decides to call a tool, the stream pauses, the tool executes, and the result feeds back into a new stream. This is how tools like Claude Code and Codex provide real-time feedback during long-running tasks.

Structured Output Parsing

Many agent tasks require structured output — JSON, YAML, or specific data formats. Use the LLM’s structured output mode (OpenAI’s response_format, Anthropic’s tool use with structured tools) to guarantee valid output. The harness can then validate the output against a Pydantic schema before passing it to downstream systems.

From Single Agent to Multi-Agent Orchestration

A single agent harness is powerful, but many real-world problems require multiple agents working together.

Agent Handoffs and Delegation Patterns

In a multi-agent system, one agent can hand off a task to another agent that specializes in a different domain. The handoff is itself a tool — the agent calls a “delegate to writer agent” tool, and the harness routes the task to the appropriate sub-agent. This pattern is used by OpenAI Agents SDK (handoffs), LangGraph (conditional edges), and Hermes Agent (delegate_task tool).

Building a Meta-Harness for Multiple Agent Types

A meta-harness orchestrates different agent types — CLI agents, browser agents, code agents, voice agents — under a single coordination layer. Projects like Omnigent (7,500+ GitHub stars) demonstrate this pattern, supporting Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Hermes, and custom agents through a unified interface. The meta-harness handles routing, state sharing, and result aggregation across heterogeneous agents.

Policy and Governance Layers

Production agent systems need guardrails. A policy layer sits between the LLM and tool execution, enforcing rules like:

  • Approval gates: Require human approval before destructive actions (file deletion, database writes, financial transactions).
  • Spend caps: Limit API costs per session, per user, or per day.
  • Tool restrictions: Block certain tools in specific contexts (no web access for sensitive data).
  • Audit logging: Record every tool call, LLM response, and decision for compliance.

Testing and Evaluating Your Agent Harness

Building the harness is only half the work. You need to verify it behaves correctly.

Synthetic Scenario Generation

Tools like Gambit generate synthetic test scenarios that exercise your agent’s capabilities. Instead of manually writing test cases, you describe the capabilities you want to test, and the scenario generator produces diverse inputs that probe edge cases, error conditions, and complex multi-step workflows.

Behavior Grading and Regression Testing

Each test scenario produces a trace of the agent’s behavior — which tools it called, in what order, what arguments it used, and what final answer it produced. A grading system compares this trace against expected behavior, flagging regressions when a code change causes the agent to take a different (worse) path. This is the agent equivalent of unit testing.

Trace Capture and Debugging

Every turn of the execution loop should be captured as a trace: the messages sent to the LLM, the tool calls made, the results returned, and the timing of each step. These traces are invaluable for debugging. When an agent makes a surprising decision, the trace shows exactly what information it had at that moment. The OpenAI Agents SDK includes built-in tracing, and you can implement your own by wrapping the execution loop with a trace recorder.

When to Build vs. When to Use Existing Frameworks

Building your own harness is educational and gives you full control, but it is not always the right choice.

Comparison of Popular Agent Frameworks

Framework Stars Key Strength Best For
OpenAI Agents SDK 28K+ Lightweight, provider-agnostic, built-in tracing Production multi-agent apps
LangGraph 12K+ Graph-based state machine, conditional routing Complex workflows with branching
CrewAI 20K+ Role-based agent teams, simple API Content generation, research pipelines
Mastra 8K+ TypeScript-native, serverless-friendly JavaScript/TypeScript ecosystems
Hermes Agent 5K+ CLI-first, skill system, cron jobs DevOps, automation, background tasks
Omnigent 7.5K+ Multi-device, policy engine, cloud sandbox Enterprise governance, multi-agent orchestration

Decision Framework for Build-vs-Buy

Build your own harness when:

  • You need deep understanding of how agents work (learning goal).
  • Your use case is simple (one model, a few tools, single user).
  • You have unique requirements that existing frameworks don’t support.
  • You want zero external dependencies and full control over the codebase.

Use an existing framework when:

  • You need production-grade reliability, tracing, and error handling out of the box.
  • Your team needs to move fast and cannot afford to build infrastructure.
  • You need multi-agent orchestration with handoffs, governance, and monitoring.
  • You want community support, documentation, and proven patterns.

The middle ground is to start with a custom harness for learning, then migrate to a framework for production. Many teams build a thin custom layer on top of the OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph, getting the best of both worlds.

Conclusion — The Future of Agent Harnesses

The agent harness is becoming the operating system of AI applications. Just as every web application needs an HTTP server, every AI application will need an agent harness. The trend is clear: from 150-line prototypes to 28K-star SDKs, from single-agent loops to multi-agent meta-harnesses with policy engines and governance layers.

The “Code as Agent Harness” paradigm suggests that code itself — with its ability to reason, act, model environments, and verify execution — is the ultimate harness. As models grow more capable, the harness’s role shifts from compensating for model limitations to enabling model capabilities. The best time to understand this architecture was yesterday. The second best time is now.

Build your own harness. Break it. Fix it. Extend it. Then decide whether to keep it or adopt a framework. Either way, you will understand agents at a level that no tutorial can teach without hands-on code.

FAQ

What is the difference between an agent harness and an agent framework?

An agent harness is the minimal runtime that manages the LLM-tool-execution loop. An agent framework is a higher-level abstraction that includes harness functionality plus additional features like multi-agent orchestration, memory systems, evaluation tools, and built-in integrations. The harness is the core; the framework is the full ecosystem.

How many lines of code does a basic agent harness need?

A functional agent harness with tool registry, LLM client, conversation memory, and execution loop can be implemented in approximately 150-200 lines of Python. The go-micro team demonstrated a working CLI agent in 150 lines, and the implementation in this tutorial is under 200 lines.

Can I use a local LLM with a custom agent harness?

Yes. The LLM client abstraction in a well-designed harness supports any OpenAI-compatible API. Local models running through Ollama, vLLM, or llama.cpp expose an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so you can point your harness at http://localhost:11434/v1 with a model like Llama 3 or Qwen 2.5.

What is a meta-harness in multi-agent systems?

A meta-harness is an orchestrator that manages multiple heterogeneous agents under a single coordination layer. It handles routing tasks to the right agent, sharing state between agents, aggregating results, and enforcing cross-agent policies. Omnigent is a prominent example of a meta-harness architecture.

How do I test an agent harness for reliability?

Test your harness using synthetic scenario generation (tools like Gambit), behavior grading that compares actual vs. expected tool-call sequences, regression testing that catches behavior changes after code modifications, and trace capture that records every LLM call and tool execution for debugging. This four-layer testing approach mirrors unit, integration, and system testing in traditional software.

item.title: OpenHarness: Universal Agent Harness for Any LLM (2026 Review)
item.description: OpenHarness is an open-source universal agent harness supporting Claude, GPT, Gemini, Ollama and any LLM under a single CLI runtime.
item.content:encoded:
OpenHarness is an open-source, CLI-first agent runtime that lets you run autonomous AI agents against any LLM — Claude, GPT-5, Gemini, Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint — without rewriting your harness each time you switch providers. As of April 2026, the HKUDS/OpenHarness project has 9,100 GitHub stars and ships 43+ built-in tools out of the box.

What Is OpenHarness? (The Name Collision Problem Explained)

OpenHarness refers to at least three distinct open-source projects that share the same name but solve the same fundamental problem: building a reusable execution layer that wraps an LLM and gives it tools, memory, permissions, and a structured agentic loop. The most prominent is HKUDS/OpenHarness (Hong Kong University of Data Science), a CLI-first runtime with 9,100 GitHub stars as of April 2026 and 43 built-in tools. A second project, AgentBoardTT/openharness, focuses on multi-provider SDK integration with explicit support for Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Ollama under a unified auth model. A third lives at OpenHarness.ai and emphasizes harness interoperability. Despite the naming confusion, all three projects share the same philosophical root: Agent = Model + Harness. The model provides intelligence; the harness provides everything else — tools, memory, lifecycle hooks, permissions, and observability. In a market projected to grow from $8.29 billion in 2025 to $12.06 billion in 2026 at a CAGR of 45.5%, building vendor-agnostic harnesses is becoming the defining engineering challenge of the AI era. Understanding which “OpenHarness” you’re working with is the first step.

Why the Name Collision Matters for Developers

When you search for “openharness agent harness” on GitHub or npm you’ll surface multiple repositories. Before committing to any of them, check the GitHub org: HKUDS for the CLI runtime, AgentBoardTT for the SDK-first multi-provider variant. This guide focuses primarily on HKUDS/OpenHarness because it has the most documented production usage, but draws comparisons from AgentBoardTT where the multi-provider support is more thoroughly tested.

HKUDS OpenHarness: The Open-Source CLI Agent Runtime

HKUDS/OpenHarness is a production-grade open-source agent harness built to make the internals of AI agent systems fully inspectable and hackable. Unlike Claude Code (which ships as a closed binary with a public SDK) or the OpenAI Agents SDK (which is vendor-locked by design), HKUDS/OpenHarness is fully open: every subsystem from the agent loop to the permission evaluator is readable and forkable. The project launched in late 2024 and reached 9,100 stars by April 2026, driven by developers frustrated with vendor lock-in. Its headline features are a 10-subsystem architecture, MCP HTTP transport support, multimodal gateway integration, a built-in personal agent called Ohmo, and a CLI that feels closer to a Unix tool than a chatbot. The philosophy is explicitly “inspector-friendly” — you can run openharness --debug and see every tool call, permission check, and LLM exchange in real time. For teams building AI products that need to audit agent behavior, this transparency is a core differentiator that neither LangChain nor any vendor-hosted harness offers at the same depth.

Installing OpenHarness in Under 5 Minutes

pip install openharness
# or from source
git clone https://github.com/HKUDS/OpenHarness && cd OpenHarness
pip install -e .
openharness --version

Once installed, configure your provider:

openharness config set provider anthropic
openharness config set api_key $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
openharness run "List all Python files in this repo and summarize what each one does"

Switching to Ollama for local inference requires only two lines:

openharness config set provider ollama
openharness config set model llama3.3:70b

No code changes. The harness abstracts the provider entirely.

Core Architecture: The 10-Subsystem Agent Harness Pattern

The 10-subsystem architecture of OpenHarness represents the most detailed public taxonomy of what a production agent harness actually does. The ten subsystems are: (1) Agent Loop — the perceive-reason-act cycle that drives execution; (2) Tool Registry — 43 built-in tools covering filesystem, web, code execution, and external APIs; (3) Knowledge & Skills — persistent fact storage and reusable task templates; (4) Plugin System — first-class extension points for custom tools and providers; (5) Permission Engine — multi-level access control from read-only to full-auto; (6) Lifecycle Hooks — pre/post hooks for every tool call and agent turn; (7) MCP Transport — Model Context Protocol support over HTTP for remote tool servers; (8) Memory Subsystem — MEMORY.md persistence plus vector-backed retrieval; (9) Multi-Agent Coordination — spawning and orchestrating sub-agents; (10) Observability — structured logging, token counting, and debug traces. This taxonomy matters because most competing harnesses implement only 4–6 of these subsystems. LangChain covers tools and memory well but has no native permission engine or lifecycle hooks. Claude Code SDK covers all ten but only for Anthropic models. OpenHarness is the only open-source harness that attempts all ten subsystems across any LLM.

The Agent Loop in Detail

The agent loop follows a strict perceive → plan → tool-call → observe → repeat cycle. Each turn, the model receives the current context window (system prompt + conversation history + tool results), generates either a response or a tool call, and the harness executes the tool and appends the result. OpenHarness adds two non-standard extensions: streaming tool-call cycles (the model can emit partial tool arguments and the harness streams the execution) and background task management (long-running tools run in a separate process with progress callbacks to the main loop). Both features address a gap in simpler harnesses where a single slow tool call (a 30-second web scrape, a database migration) would block the entire agent.

Permission Engine: Multi-Level Access Control

OpenHarness ships three permission modes: read-only (file reads and web fetches only), confirm (all writes prompt the user), and auto (full autonomous execution). This mirrors Claude Code’s permission model but extends it to any LLM provider — you can run a local Llama model in confirm mode with the same safety guarantees you’d expect from a closed-source harness. A fourth mode, allowlist, lets you define per-tool permissions at the granularity of individual filesystem paths or API endpoints.

Universal LLM Support — Every Provider, One Harness

Universal LLM support is OpenHarness’s most commercially important feature: a single harness configuration works across Anthropic Claude (all versions), OpenAI GPT-4o and GPT-5, Google Gemini 2.0 and 2.5, Mistral, Kimi, GLM-4, and any server that speaks the OpenAI-compatible chat completion API — including self-hosted Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, and Together AI. In 2026, 65% of global organisations use generative AI tools, and most enterprises run more than one LLM provider for cost, compliance, or capability reasons. A harness that forces you to pick one provider creates a hidden long-term cost: every time the model landscape shifts (GPT-5 arrives, a new Gemini model drops), you rewrite your harness. OpenHarness avoids this by normalizing all providers behind a single ProviderAdapter interface. Tool calls, streaming, token counting, and error handling are handled by the adapter; your agent code never sees the difference. The AgentBoardTT variant takes this further with explicit benchmarks showing sub-100ms provider switching latency in tests across Claude, GPT, and Gemini.

Supported Providers and Configuration

Provider Auth Method Streaming Tool Calls Notes
Anthropic Claude API key Yes Yes claude-opus-4-7, sonnet-4-6, haiku-4-5
OpenAI GPT API key Yes Yes gpt-4o, gpt-5, o3
Google Gemini Service account / key Yes Yes gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-2.5-pro
Ollama (local) None Yes Yes Any Ollama-compatible model
vLLM / LM Studio API key optional Yes Partial OpenAI-compatible endpoints
Kimi / GLM-4 API key Yes Yes Chinese model providers
Together AI API key Yes Yes Hosted open-source models

Switching providers requires only editing ~/.openharness/config.yaml or passing --provider and --model flags at the CLI. No code changes in your agent logic.

Built-in Tools, Skills, and the Ohmo Personal Agent

OpenHarness ships 43 built-in tools across six categories, making it immediately useful without writing any tool integrations. The six categories are: Filesystem (read, write, glob, grep, tree — 8 tools), Web (fetch, search, screenshot, crawl — 7 tools), Code (execute Python/JS/Bash, lint, test runner — 9 tools), External APIs (GitHub, Slack, Linear, calendar — 10 tools), Memory (save fact, recall, summarize conversation — 5 tools), and System (process management, environment, cron — 4 tools). The 43-tool count matches what Claude Code ships, but unlike Claude Code’s tools (which are tightly coupled to the Anthropic SDK), OpenHarness tools are provider-agnostic — they work identically whether the underlying model is Claude or Llama. Beyond the built-in tools, OpenHarness ships a Skills system: reusable task templates that combine multiple tools into named workflows. A skills/deploy.yaml file, for example, can encode your entire deploy pipeline as a skill that the agent can invoke by name. This is the harness equivalent of shell aliases, but semantically grounded — the agent understands what a skill does, not just how to call it.

Ohmo: The Built-in Personal Agent

Ohmo is OpenHarness’s built-in personal agent, designed to be the “always-on” companion that manages your development environment. Unlike running openharness run "..." for one-off tasks, Ohmo maintains persistent context across sessions, remembers your project structure, tracks in-progress tasks, and proactively surfaces reminders. Under the hood, Ohmo uses the Memory subsystem (MEMORY.md persistence + optional vector retrieval) and runs on a configurable heartbeat — by default checking in every 30 minutes to look for new tasks, expiring reminders, or stalled background jobs. Ohmo is provider-agnostic: you can back it with Claude for complex reasoning and fall back to a local Ollama model when offline.

# Start Ohmo as a background daemon
openharness ohmo start --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-6
# Ask Ohmo something
openharness ohmo ask "What tasks are in progress in this repo?"
# Stop the daemon
openharness ohmo stop

OpenHarness vs Other Harnesses: Head-to-Head Comparison

The right agent harness depends on whether you prioritize vendor flexibility, developer experience, production reliability, or research transparency. In 2026, the main contenders are OpenHarness (HKUDS), Claude Code SDK (Anthropic), LangChain/LangGraph, and the OpenAI Agents SDK. OpenHarness is the only fully open-source option that supports all major LLM providers under a single runtime, making it the strongest choice for teams that cannot commit to a single vendor. Claude Code SDK delivers the best developer experience for Anthropic-only stacks — it’s tightly integrated, well-documented, and production-hardened. LangChain covers the widest range of integrations (databases, vector stores, document loaders) but its abstractions have historically leaked at scale. The OpenAI Agents SDK is the fastest path to production if your stack is 100% OpenAI, but offers no path to provider migration. Gartner projects 40% of enterprise applications will include task-specific AI agents by end of 2026 — which means the harness decision you make today will affect your architecture for years.

When to Choose OpenHarness Over Claude Code

If your team uses more than one LLM provider — either today or plausibly in the next 12 months — OpenHarness is the correct harness choice. The switching cost from Claude Code to OpenHarness is high once you’ve built against the Anthropic SDK’s agent primitives. The switching cost from OpenHarness to a different provider is nearly zero. The key question to ask: “If Anthropic prices doubled tomorrow, could we switch models without rewriting our agent?”

Who Should Use OpenHarness in 2026?

OpenHarness is the right tool for four categories of developer in 2026. First, multi-cloud enterprise teams building agents that need to run on different models in different regions or compliance environments — OpenHarness’s unified auth model and provider-agnostic tool layer handles this cleanly. Second, research teams who need full transparency into agent internals — every subsystem is inspectable, every tool call is logged, and the debug output is structured for analysis. Third, developers building agent-powered developer tools who want a production harness without vendor lock-in and with a CLI interface that fits naturally into existing shell workflows. Fourth, cost-sensitive startups who want to run agents on Ollama or open-weight models locally during development and switch to Claude or GPT in production — OpenHarness makes this a config change. OpenHarness is probably not the right choice for teams that are already heavily invested in the Claude Code SDK and have no multi-provider requirements, or for teams using LangChain’s extensive document-loader and vector-store ecosystem extensively. The LLM market is projected to grow from $4.5 billion in 2023 to $82.1 billion by 2033 — the teams that invest in provider-agnostic infrastructure today will have far more flexibility as that market matures.

Teams That Should Stick with Claude Code SDK

Teams building exclusively on Anthropic models with complex extended thinking workflows, tight MCP integrations using stdio transport, or deep reliance on Claude-specific features (citations, computer use, vision-heavy workflows) will find Claude Code SDK more production-ready today. OpenHarness’s Claude adapter is solid but not as deeply tested as the native SDK.

Getting Started with OpenHarness (Quick Setup Guide)

Getting a working OpenHarness agent running takes under 10 minutes from a fresh machine. The harness requires Python 3.11+ and installs via pip. After installation, the openharness init command scaffolds a project directory with a config file, a MEMORY.md file for persistence, and a skills/ directory for reusable task templates. The first time you run an agent, OpenHarness will prompt you for your LLM provider credentials and store them in ~/.openharness/config.yaml. From there, you can run one-shot tasks via openharness run "...", start a persistent Ohmo session via openharness ohmo start, or build a custom agent by importing the SDK: from openharness import Agent, ToolRegistry. The SDK path is useful when you need to embed OpenHarness inside a larger application — a FastAPI service, a CI/CD pipeline, or a Slack bot — without exposing the CLI interface. OpenHarness’s Agent class takes a provider, a model, a tool_registry, and a permission_mode, and exposes a simple agent.run(prompt) method that handles the full agentic loop internally.

Step-by-Step Setup

# 1. Install
pip install openharness

# 2. Initialize a project
mkdir my-agent && cd my-agent
openharness init

# 3. Configure your provider (interactive)
openharness config setup
# Prompts: provider, api_key, model, permission_mode

# 4. Run your first agent task
openharness run "Find all TODO comments in this directory and create a summary report"

# 5. Switch to a different provider
openharness config set provider ollama && openharness config set model qwen3:32b
openharness run "Same task, different model — no code changes required"

Using the Python SDK

from openharness import Agent, ToolRegistry
from openharness.providers import AnthropicProvider

registry = ToolRegistry.defaults()  # loads all 43 built-in tools
provider = AnthropicProvider(model="claude-sonnet-4-6")

agent = Agent(
    provider=provider,
    tool_registry=registry,
    permission_mode="confirm",
    memory_path="./MEMORY.md"
)

result = agent.run("Analyze this codebase and identify the three riskiest files")
print(result.response)

Swapping AnthropicProvider for OllamaProvider(model="llama3.3:70b") requires no other changes.

FAQ

Q: Is OpenHarness the same as Claude Code? No. OpenHarness (HKUDS) is an independent open-source project that supports any LLM provider, including Claude. Claude Code is Anthropic’s own CLI and SDK, which only works with Anthropic models. OpenHarness is architecturally similar to Claude Code — both have a CLI, a permission engine, and a 10-subsystem harness model — but OpenHarness is vendor-agnostic and fully open-source.

Q: Can I use OpenHarness with a local model via Ollama? Yes. OpenHarness has first-class Ollama support. Set provider: ollama and model: llama3.3:70b (or any Ollama-compatible model) in your config, and the harness will route all LLM calls to your local Ollama server. All 43 built-in tools, the permission engine, and the memory subsystem work identically with local models.

Q: How does OpenHarness handle tool calls for models that don’t support native function calling? OpenHarness includes a fallback tool-call parser that works with models that produce structured JSON in their response text rather than native function-call tokens. This is used automatically for models that don’t support the OpenAI tool-call format, enabling tool-use with older or smaller models that lack native support.

Q: What is the difference between HKUDS/OpenHarness and AgentBoardTT/openharness? HKUDS/OpenHarness is the more mature project with 9,100 stars, a full CLI, 43 built-in tools, and the Ohmo personal agent. AgentBoardTT/openharness is a lighter-weight SDK-first project focused on multi-provider benchmarking with explicit latency measurements across providers. If you want a full production runtime, use HKUDS. If you want a thin multi-provider abstraction layer for your own agent framework, AgentBoardTT may be a better fit.

Q: Is OpenHarness production-ready in 2026? HKUDS/OpenHarness is production-ready for teams that accept it’s a 2-year-old project with a smaller support ecosystem than LangChain or Claude Code SDK. It runs reliably in CI/CD pipelines, has a stable CLI interface, and its core subsystems (agent loop, tools, permissions) are well-tested. The MCP transport and multi-agent coordination features are newer and carry more risk. For high-stakes production deployments, plan for more testing than you’d budget for Claude Code SDK.
